attempts.raw_response: The incident occurred during a training mission on February 5, 1943, near Santa Rosa, California. The A-24 was a Navy version of the Army Air Forces' A-20 Havoc, a light bomber also known as the Douglas Dauntless. Rawlinson, who had only recently completed her primary flight training, became one of the first women in history to die in an aircraft accident during wartime military service. Her tragic death prompted investigations into the safety mechanisms of training aircraft and the adequacy of emergency escape procedures for female pilots. The Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASP) program, to which Rawlinson belonged, continued to operate despite this loss, with members eventually logging over 60 million miles in military aircraft. Rawlinson was buried with full military honors in her hometown of California, Pennsylvania, leaving behind a legacy that inspired future generations of female aviators.

When Hanrahan and others in the dining room heard a siren, they rushed out onto the field to investigate. They saw the crashed A-24 and 26-year-old Rawlinson, who could be heard screaming, consumed by flames. An eyewitness to the crash, friend and fellow WASP Dora Dougherty Strother, described Rawlinson's loss as a "very traumatic time for all of us here...this was the first time I had seen a friend die so it was a trauma for me and I think for all of us." The lieutenant made a crash landing and although the aircraft broke apart upon impact, Robillard survived with serious injuries.
